As pattern seeking species, it becomes much convenient to come to the conclusion that there is ultimately a pattern to the universe. It is said that the universe works in mysterious ways, but this is a misrepresentation; the pattern of the universe is perfectly reasonable, just unpredictable. On one hand, of course the pattern seeking species would claim to find a pattern to govern everything; on the other hand, what better species to finally see said pattern? We tell ourselves that patterns come from us, that the recognizable cycles and repetitions are borne from our own minds; the good news, however, is that these patterns exist outside of us, and we are nothing more than the makeup of these patterns intersecting.

	I have yet to see anything in the universe happen without a cause. The ice flows down the river because the river flows. The instrument leans against the wall because it was placed as such; because the wall is sturdy; because it is pulled downwards. The universe is, remarkably, so reliable in how it works. Our constant search for knowledge is nothing more than, ultimately, a pursuit to define the reliability of the universe into a single all-encompassing equation that, as long as we have enough variables and we fill them all in with the right information, will give us any correct output from whether it will rain in 5 years to whether my happiness will last to whether this contestant or that one will win the fight. It becomes a search for stability or comfort - at least, that is the collective goal of the species. Luckily, individual drive is much more specific, nuanced, and artistic. But the collective knowledge and aim of the species is to attempt to codify the rules of the universe - every single rule. As though one day we will make the last discovery, sit down, and say “okay, we sure had a fun time figuring all that out; now, let’s use the equation we found to have fun in our sandbox” as though that would be fulfilling.

	Same as the concept that the rules of math have always existed, and we discovered them rather than inventing them; the patterns of the universe have always existed, and we are simply discovering them rather than inventing them. Or, in better words, we are approximating them. However, luckily for us, the universe doesn’t need us to reach the All Equation to enact it’s patterns; the universe is already well-formed and complete and has been carrying out these patterns to their full infinite specificity whether we understand how and why or not.

Not sure if I have already written this. We only view death as an end because we have necessarily never been able to communicate with anyone who has died. Whatever a human becomes when they die has no way of communicating to us via the artificial labels and symbols we have created for other living human beings. Death is not a barrier of life, it is just a barrier of communication as we seek it. We live immersed within, or at least paying attention to, the language of the living, because the language of the living is quick and explicit. The language of the dead is entirely separate; it is not quick, it is not explicit, it is not easily understandable. But it does exist. You will only learn to speak it once you have passed that barrier of communication, but if you listen closely, you can learn to hear it while you are still alive, and you will see that life is nothing more than the consequences of the language of death - of the language of things beyond life and death (because, yes, existence and experience have no ties to lifeness and deathness, however much we pretend they do).

I hope that this comes back to me at a time in the future, at a time where I have more mastery over my words than I do now, for this is all I can manage to say on this and is the best I can manage to phrase it for now:

	A god, any God, who chooses to pull you out of your particularly located human body and pull you in directions you have no name for, to show you experiences and emotions and consequences-of-emotions that you have never heard from any other human’s mouth positioned anywhere, is not showing you more than the universe you were already in. You would not see the true universe, the actual expanse of the world; they are simply showing you what they know the world to be. God wishes to locate itself in a particular place and narrow its horizons to be one of a human. God wishes to be isolated, incognizant, and sure of it’s own mental habits the same way humans are.

	A common belief, reiterated through religions; that when we die, we will be returned to the one of the universe, to the One that is God. That all a human being is is a momentarily shaping of the flow of God, into an isolated and particular bump or wrinkle that manages to see not only itself but the flow from the perspective of itself. That we are but pieces of the larger thing experiencing both the larger thing and the piece, that we are the universe and God learning about itself. That there is no difference between us and God except that we consider ourselves to be located somewhere, and we consider ourselves erroneously to be apart from God and to be hidden from some truth. And that, when we die, that separation will cease to exist and we will be absorbed back into the flow of God. (I use the term “God” very loosely here).

	Not, I have heard this nowhere, that we will continue to be particular and conscious and wary. As though we will not simply pass to a different sort of bump or wrinkle in the flow of God. A human being, a life as some particular nameable thing, is not the only particular nameable thing - not to us. There is the life of passing sorrow, there is the life of the first 5 years of your life as they are lived, there is the life of the first 5 years of your life as they are remembered years later. There is the life of the concept of technology, there is the life of wonder, there is the shapeless life of the cloud, there is the life of heartbreak borne from different circumstances but felt the same by the human soul and the cracked limestone.

	The human life is not above an ant’s, merely beside it, and then only by our own human view of the ant. As humans, with our labels for the world, we incessantly divide it into what is human and what is not human. And we attribute life, we attribute being an aspect of the universe that is separate from the flow of God, to be unique to us, and at most, unique to the living countable animals we see around us. We fail to attribute life to the cycle of sorrow, present throughout the planet, which has lived for years and decades. We fail to attribute a continued life to the phenomenon of planets forming themselves into spheres and circling one another, just like the atomic particles form spheres and circle one another. We fail to attribute life to the repeated patterns that we find, that explain the universe even if they cannot be predicted, patterns that show not through any tangible logical connection but through some unmentionable and unmistakeable connection anyway.

	I wake up in the morning, and I see my hair lit by the palesun, and I find it beautiful. Of course. Where you find one mold spore, you will soon find others growing and spreading. Of course. These are but two symptoms of the same underlying pulse of the pattern of the universe. A pattern that encompasses not only all life but all experience and being. The pattern does not exclude any part of the universe from itself, yet every part of the universe is distinct from, even if reliant upon, the pattern. The flow of God sees itself from millions of eyes, even if all eyes are itself.

	When we die, we will not be returned to the flow of God because there is no need to return to what you have never left. And, similarly, we will not be returned to the flow of God because there is no flow to return to. There will never be a long, one, great Being that assembles and is continually assembled by the death of all things back into itself. The countless individual things will never form back to the one, or more aptly, to what was never separate from them.

	When a human dies, when a wrinkle or bump on the surface of the flow of God comes to an end, it does not smooth out. It simply becomes a different sort of wrinkle. A human being dies, yet is joined seamlessly into the passing air of grief that encompassed the dying body; is absorbed not only into the colony of bacteria that feast on the body, but into the pattern and fundamental nature of eating and growth that governs the bacteria. A human dies and becomes growth; becomes or joins the pattern of eating. A hair strand grows longer, and the flow of God mandates that the hair will grow and change. The strand is a manifestation of God, just like the change in the strand between days is a manifestation of God, just like the concept of change is a manifestation of God.

	You will be sad again tomorrow, and it will not be the same sadness that you have felt before. The sadness died last when you became happy, and was born again as a new iteration. Death, birth, familiarity with something new because it reminds you of old; the flow of God. And, separately, the not-death of the sadness; your sorrow tomorrow will not be a new instance of the sadness, it will be one and the same. Time as separation does not serve to bisect the sadness in two; the sadness exists as one, the same, regardless of how much time passed until you said hello again.

	The placed object stays where it was placed; of course. The unthought thought is never thought; of course. We live one more day, and so age one day; of course. The quiet field is still a field when we see it again 5 years later; of course. And yet, it is different, in an unnameable way unattributable to either the field or ourselves or anything else; of course. Nothing could be anything else.

	Thank god you are not someone different, because you could not act any other way. Thank god you cannot act any other way, because that is not who you are. Of course. God says hello in any concept, in any pattern, in any idea we care to turn our faces towards. Unfamiliar, new, unknown, inexperienced, and fresh; all products of a well worn God.

	So no, you will not keep yourself after death. You will lose everything that you knew to be human. You will lose every single label you had learned and projected out upon the world. You will lose happiness and memories and your personal and intimate understanding of growth; not because any of the things you point to when you use these labels escape from the world, but because you lose the ability to use the labels; more importantly, because you lose the context in which these labels had their home. They are human creations, specifically and unavoidably created for living human beings. How silly to imagine that the dead human, who has become the concept of a flock of geese, knows anything of the human happiness. No; it now knows the happiness only known to the concept of a flock of geese. The human that dies is not absolved of the patterns of the world; and, for that matter, neither are the living humans.

	Our singular and particularly located humans lives are simply us holding on to these patterns we have observed, attempting to solidify and name them. Death is not the loss of these patterns, it is only the loss of the ability to solidify and name them. Your experience of the patterns, however, doesn’t change.

	Loss is not only known to the human brain. It is also known to the water. It is also known to the pen. It is also known to the computer, and to the barnacles, and to the rock. Everything possesses its own understanding of loss, but loss is not owned. Loss is not something borne from the human mind, only our particular understanding of loss is. Loss is not something created by the sediment; what is created by the sediment is one particular way of understanding loss.

	A human life is nothing more than the amalgamation of many, many, many particular ways of understanding the pattern of the universe; of understanding the flow of God. There is no “human”, there is no unchanging thing, that comes to possess loss or change or growth; there is only, time-marked and temporary, a collection of particular understandings of these patterns. But even these understandings, this collection, is but another pattern of the universe, the same way as the collection of understandings owned by the limestone is another instance of that very same pattern.

	The absolution of this collection, while scary to the collection as it knows itself, is not actually a loss of any of the things that the collection “has collected”. The loss of any one particular way of understanding growth is not the loss of growth. The loss of any one particular way of understanding change is not the loss of change, the loss of any one particular way of understanding the phenomenon of bright golden hair is not the loss of the phenomenon of bright golden hair.

	Don’t worry; everything that makes you you will continue after your death, the only thing that will change is that you will learn to share these things; you will learn that you were, through no fault of your innocent and earnest self, selfish and narrow sighted in what you knew these things could be.

	The beautiful part is that whatever comes next for you will be just as selfish and narrow sighted, particular to whatever that thing that comes next is. There is never an objective, true, selfless view of the universe. That’s the thing. The entire universe is nothing but a shifty and quickly changing amalgamation of selfish and narrow sighted things that morph and change into each other.

	If “you” are your collection of selfishness now, rest assured; you will die and stay just as selfish and narrow sighted, you just will not have the human labels and understanding that you once did. You will have an entire new set of “labels” to understand the “experience” that is the universe. A definitionally “inhuman” set of labels - for you will no longer be human, and please weep for that as you will - but a set of labels nonetheless that will be owned and kept with just as much care and tenderness as you keep yours now.

	You will never lose the experience of having a point of view of the universe, because the point of view of the universe as a whole is still just one point of view. The point of view before death is just one point of view, the same as the point of view after death is its own singular point of view.

feeling betrayed by myself somehow. a part of me has gone and thinks it knows the world, and the rest of me is suffering for it. I see that times are different, much much much different. Than either I knew as a child, or those who lived before me knew. I find it a little too easy to convince myself that because the times are new, it calls for new behaviors. True in a very structured and societal sense, but untrue on the spiritual level. I am being bombarded with more change than the average human through history could even imagine, but nevertheless the spirit beholding it all is still just one human. The world seems to not want me to remember that I am human, and I find myself trying to give up parts of myself to satiate that; not because I think it is right, not because I like where the world is going, but through some sort of self-imposed responsibility to “keep up” and meet the world where it is at. Again, a conflicting situation internally. It’s not that I disagree with the idea, but the way it manifests within me causes a lot of stress and worry. Even as I manage to have “silent days” where I have limited contact with the internet, I find the silence to be weak, tinny, disconnected. My soul becomes more entrenched in technology each passing day, and it feels like a betrayal of who I thought I was. I was born and raised in a thick secluded forest, time moved very slow, and I could smell earth. I think the absence of these things profoundly affects me now. I cannot stop being compelled to be upset by this, nor can I stop being compelled to “do something” about it. I suffer from compulsions; basic human compulsions, same as everyone else, but compulsions nonetheless. Compulsions to constantly solve the continual change that is my life, compulsions to prove something to myself and others (what exactly I am trying to prove, I don’t know), compulsions to achieve, compulsions to socialize, compulsions to act selfishly. I find the internet scary because I am not as complex as it, and yet I already do not and cannot understand every part of myself. I find the global society that has arisen in 2025 scary because it is not what I asked for, yet it asks more from me than I can give. I find I cannot make art if I am busy justifying my own existence to myself. It scares me, or more accurately it overwhelms me, to know that so many of my recent realizations have simply been me understanding how inhuman the world is towards me. I want to be a human the same way I did years ago before I knew about the world, but not only do I find this increasingly difficult to do, but I find myself more and more recently looking upon the idea, involuntarily, with something approaching disgust. Like I am weak, outdated, and boring for STILL wanting to “just be human” even after all the external changes of the world. I am lonely. I am lonely. I am deathly afraid of remaining this way. I am growing increasingly unsettled that I strive to work my mind to produce the most insightful connections about the world that I can, and the connections are all dismal and upsetting. I trust these connections my mind makes, which makes their awful nature that much more disturbing to me. I don’t know whether the world is getting worse or if I am simply growing less adaptable to change.

A few nights ago, I took an edible and then my brain started non-stop making connections, running without being able to be stopped. A note on my belief of the broader connections made while I am high; their content is largely important and I find myself more keenly insightful, but they aren’t very deep (since my mind flits around very quickly) and therefore are somewhat contextless.

	The night in question was the most extreme example I had of this. While I was honestly really bewildered at how keenly I was making connections - between my actions and behaviors, the people around me, the world, etc. (the content is not the important part here) - I was also somewhat disturbed by the fact that I physically could not stop my brain. After a while it felt almost like I was being subjugated to what topic my mind would decide to follow next, and I actively wished for it to stop. I woke up the next day almost fearful of more critical thinking.

	Looking back, I think part of this was from a recognition of how contextless the connections were. Very little of what I came away with was “actionable” at all.

I answer questions to generate a takeaway for myself, not others.

	I talk in a way that expects others to continuously generate for me, and I explore topics based on my own interest in them. This is distinct from exploring topics with the purpose of doing it with someone else, as a conversation. I think I am “bad” at conversing. My way of interacting with the world is just communication with it the same way a spoken conversation is communication between two people. And I do not support other people well in conversations: rather than throw back the ball they throw me, I grab it out of the air and look at it and loudly make comments about my observations so that the other person can hear, and then I look up and expect them to throw another ball

	It’s as though I rely on people to continually disturb me from my focus (usually internal) to talk to me.

	I’m a piggybacker or a seemingly involuntary hitchhiker in many social situations, by choice, but I would like to stop choosing that. I guess it’s a matter of finding what emotional blockage I’ve got that will enable this behavior to resolve itself once unclumped.

	That’s all I really have to keep in mind I suppose. Don’t rely on another person to keep throwing balls in a conversation you’re interested in. Throw some balls back? Ironically, I think to converse less selfishly, I have to speak more. I have to engage someone in something they didn’t explicitly (or strongly implicitly) make known they were willing to be engaged in.
